
ARIMA, XGBoost, and GARCH therefore do not disappear from the rebuild. Their Part 1 questions are answered. The autoregressive idea becomes an evaluated component of the preferred model. A bounded XGBoost model using only dates and recursively generated lags offers no clear evidential advantage over the simpler evaluated models. The volatility question is handled on the count scale through negative-binomial predictive dispersion rather than a continuous-return GARCH model.

## XGBoost v2: reserved for Part 2

The more ambitious XGBoost question is not rejected; it is larger than this report. It would combine the NYPD series with point-in-time contextual streams describing weather, movement, public events, infrastructure disruption, news, and wider societal conditions. Constructing those features without future leakage requires a separately documented source inventory, historical ingestion strategy, data model, licensing review, and spatiotemporal evaluation design. That work will be explored in a separate document rather than compressed into this completed exploratory report.

## Data-platform feasibility

The original report also left SQL Server, Azure, and “big data” as empty headings. At the present scale, the answer is architectural restraint. The pinned project contains tens of thousands of records and a daily analytical series of only 7,305 complete-year observations. It does not need a distributed data platform to render a reproducible report.

```{r infrastructure-table, results='asis'}
infrastructure_table <- data.frame(
  Stage = c("Current report", "Automated refresh", "Shared operational service", "Distributed big-data platform"),
  Appropriate.design = c(
    "Pinned CSV/JSON evidence, Python analysis, and reproducible PDF rendering",
    "Scheduled acquisition plus a small relational store with raw, core, mart, and audit schemas",
    "SQL Server or Azure SQL only when multiple users, access control, monitoring, and service continuity become real requirements",
    "Not justified for this report; evaluate separately if Part 2 ingests high-volume, heterogeneous, time-sensitive contextual streams"
  ),
  Decision = c("Keep", "Future option", "Conditional option", "Separate study"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
names(infrastructure_table)[[2L]] <- "Appropriate design"
knitr::kable(
  infrastructure_table, format = report_table_format, booktabs = report_is_latex,
  align = if (report_is_latex) c("l", "p{8.2cm}", "l") else c("l", "l", "l")
)
```

If the work becomes an automated service, a relational design should preserve the same units already enforced here: immutable raw snapshots; separate incident, victim, and known-offender core tables; daily and geographic analytical marts; forecast-origin and prediction tables; and a manifest/audit layer containing source URLs, retrieval times, hashes, and validation outcomes. Azure SQL is a possible managed implementation, not a methodological upgrade. No cloud resource, SQL Server instance, or distributed platform was created for this report. A materially larger platform may be justified by XGBoost v2, but that decision belongs to Part 2 and must be based on its source volume, update cadence, history, and reproducibility requirements.

# Limitations, lessons, and further work

The verified core has several boundaries:

- It describes NYPD administrative records, not every shooting or every affected person.
- Incident, victim, and known-offender tables answer different questions and have different coverage.
- Known-offender information is incomplete and potentially non-random; it is not evidence of conviction.
- Calendar, borough, and demographic patterns are descriptive. They do not establish mechanisms or policy effects.
- The 2020 borough rates use one matching population denominator and should not be extrapolated across the entire series.
- Boroughs are broad aggregations that conceal neighbourhood variation and changing exposure.
- The 2020 tract-income analysis is ecological. ACS estimates carry sampling uncertainty, observed tract rates can be unstable, neighbouring tracts are not statistically independent, and the association does not identify individual exposure or a causal mechanism.
- The coordinate map shows accumulated recorded incidents without a time-varying local population denominator. Point density is not personal risk.
- Fatal-incident known-offender analyses cover only incidents with at least one linked published record; one in three fatal incidents has no such link in this snapshot.
- Central Park is one fixed weather station; it does not measure block-level conditions at every incident location. The temperature model controls broad calendar structure but not every time-varying factor associated with weather and shootings.
- Federal holidays are a defined legal calendar, not every culturally important date in New York. Holiday estimates are repeated-date associations and named-holiday samples are small.
- Championship dates describe three nationally salient series, not all sports, local attendance, home-team participation, or event intensity. Their matched comparisons are not causal effects.
- Crowd Counting Consortium coverage begins in 2017, changes across collection phases, depends on publicly discoverable reports, and occupies most calendar days in the NYC subset. An event-day indicator cannot represent the number, size, location, claim, or policing of those events.
- Forecast accuracy is evaluated at twelve 2022-2025 origins after model selection on 2018-2021 origins. That is stronger than an in-sample fit but remains a modest evaluation sample spanning one recent regime. The primary model's nominal 80% interval is conservative, and citywide accuracy does not establish precinct-level usefulness.
- No weather, event, or political-crowd variable enters the forecast because its future value or reporting process is not reliably known at the forecast origin. Associative context is not automatically a leakage-safe predictor.
- The author is interpreting public administrative data without claiming local institutional or lived-experience authority.
- The partial 2026 record may change as later periods are published and must not be mixed with complete years.

The main lesson carried from the original analysis is simple: verify the unit of observation before naming a count. The rebuild now uses the shootings table for incidents, the victim table for victim records, and the offender table for known-offender records. Most of the original questions survive; their denominators and claims become more precise.

The maintained analysis, report figures, and numerical claims reconcile with the pinned evidence layer described in the appendix.

\clearpage

# Conclusion

The rebuilt report preserves the original project's intended direction while replacing fragile counts with maintained analytical units. Across complete years, the record shows a long decline, a sharp 2020 discontinuity, and another decline through 2025. The first half of 2026 is slightly below the equivalent 2025 window. Summer, weekends, and late-night hours contain more recorded incidents after fair calendar denominators are applied. Matching 2020 denominators changes borough, precinct, and tract questions from raw rankings into bounded rate comparisons. Within that common 2020 frame, recorded incident rates fall across higher-income tract quartiles and have a negative rank association with tract median household income; the relationship remains ecological and non-causal.

The person tables answer narrower questions than the incident table. Fatal incidents and fatal victim records are different measures. Known-offender distributions cover only published linked records, and one in three fatal incidents has no such link in this snapshot. Those absences are part of the finding, not rows to hide before plotting demographics.

Context becomes useful only after its sampling frame is explicit. Season, temperature, named holidays, three championship series, and political-crowd days do not collapse into one common effect. Their patterns are heterogeneous, their coverage differs, and every estimate remains associative.

Forecasting reaches a similarly bounded conclusion. A dynamic count ensemble supersedes Prophet in this report because it better matches the data-generating scale and produced lower rolling-origin error at both operational horizons. Yet an average error near one and a half incidents per day, conservative intervals, and a citywide target leave a large gap between “best evaluated here” and “ready to direct operations.” The honest result is useful but modest: the near future has some predictable local level and calendar structure, while much of the day-to-day variation remains unresolved.

The central lesson is therefore not that one sophisticated method rescued the old report. It is that the questions survived once their units, denominators, source universes, comparison windows, and uncertainty were made explicit. That is what turns the unfinished graduate exercise into a defensible exploratory report.

\clearpage

# How this report was made: operator, agents, and evidence

## The project before the agents

The research question, original report, source archive, and ambition began with Arthur Dominic Blanc. The early project was intentionally larger than the course checklist. It explored not only the supplied shooting record but also weather, public events, forecasting, and possible data-platform directions. The author later described the governing instinct plainly: graduate work should feel like a real project, not a demonstration that isolated aircraft parts can be assembled.

That ambition produced useful questions and an unfinished evidence system. The original report mislabeled victim-record rows as shooting incidents, left several contextual sources under-documented, relied too heavily on an in-sample Prophet view, and sometimes stretched descriptive patterns toward explanation. The rebuild did not begin with a blank prompt. It began with those authored choices, mistakes, files, and unresolved questions.

## What the operator directed

The operator's role was not limited to requesting a polished document. Arthur Dominic Blanc:

- supplied the original reports, code, datasets, feedback, and project history;
- insisted that the incident key and analytical unit be treated as foundational evidence;
- required the refreshed edition to preserve the original ambition without preserving unsupported conclusions;
- chose the public byline and visual relationship to ardrblanc.com;
- set boundaries around causality, demographic interpretation, publication, and disclosure;
- corrected omissions and rejected work that looked impressive but displaced the useful deliverable;
- approved the distinction between the completed Part 1 report and the separate contextual XGBoost v2 programme; and
- retained authority over every public claim and the decision to publish.

Those directions changed the work. When an early rebuild treated presentation as success while leaving a material issue outside the useful artifact, the operator required the deliverable first and the critique second. When prerequisites or local tools were missing, the operator required explicit notice rather than silent installation. These were not cosmetic preferences; they became part of the report's evidence and production discipline.

## What the AI systems contributed

AI assistance operated across more than one period and system. The project credits OpenAI GPT-3 and Anthropic Claude Opus 4 for owner-identified work on or around the original report. Arthur Dominic Blanc's named **Codex-1** agent and later OpenAI Codex sessions supported the rebuild. The GPT-5.6 family - Sol, Terra, and Luna - is credited for agent work including repository inspection, data auditing, implementation, test construction, source reconciliation, visual design, draft prose, packaging, and quality checks.

The systems accelerated work that would have been unrealistic to repeat manually at the same breadth: comparing historical and current sources, tracing transformations, generating and testing repair code, reviewing dozens of rendered pages, rebuilding contextual sampling frames, evaluating forecasting alternatives, and maintaining a publication ledger across code, evidence, prose, and design.

That acceleration did not make every output correct. Agent proposals were hypotheses until they matched the pinned data and passed review. Generated code was subject to tests. Generated prose was subject to source and claim review. A successful render established that a file could be produced; it did not establish that the human or analytical interpretation was true.

## A contribution and acceptance ledger

| Phase | Operator contribution | AI contribution | Acceptance evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Original work | Question, scope, coursework decisions, source selection, initial analysis | GPT-3 and Claude Opus 4 contributions identified by the owner | Archived reports, source files, and owner account |
| Evidence repair | Analytical priorities, correction requirements, claim boundaries, approval gates | Data audits, acquisition and analysis code, tests, reconciliation, model comparisons | Pinned manifests, hashes, automated tests, and reviewed findings |
| Public report | Byline, narrative purpose, sensitive-content rules, final judgments | Figure production, layout, draft prose, PDF and web implementation | Numerical reconciliation and rendered-page review |
| Kindle edition | Approval to publish, disclosure choices, credits, pricing and access strategy | Cover system, front matter, eBook conversion, accessibility and package checks | EPUB/KPF validation and owner review in Amazon tooling |

The ledger is intentionally role-based. Vendor names do not explain authorship, and model availability alone does not establish contribution. Where task records are retained, they are the preferred source for assigning a model to a specific action.

## What the agents could not decide

No model could decide why this project mattered to its author, which errors deserved candid public treatment, how much personal context could be disclosed, whether a sensitive demographic chart should remain, or when the evidence was sufficient to carry the author's name. The agents could recommend wording and safeguards. They could not grant themselves permission to publish, convert a candidate result into an approved claim, or assume responsibility for the consequences.

The author likewise did not perform every mechanical step alone. The completed edition depends on a volume of iterative inspection, code generation, comparison, and document production that the earlier one-person course schedule could not sustain. AI assistance changed what was practically achievable, but it did not remove the need to understand and defend the result.

## The counterfactual

This edition is neither the output of a person pressing a button nor the output of an autonomous model. Remove the operator and there is no original inquiry, source archive, research purpose, contextual judgment, acceptance standard, approval, or accountable interpretation. Remove the AI systems and the rebuild does not reach its present breadth, speed, or density of iterative checking within the available time.

The dependence is real but not symmetrical. The agents supplied scale, alternatives, and production capacity. Arthur Dominic Blanc supplied authority, direction, context, and responsibility. If either side had been absent, this report would not exist in its present form.

## Responsibility after collaboration

Arthur Dominic Blanc is the author, final editor, and publisher of this edition. He is responsible for verifying the public claims, correcting errors, and deciding whether the report should remain available. AI systems are credited contributors and production tools; they are not rights holders, accountable publishers, or institutional endorsers.

## Corrections

The preferred correction channel is the public project repository at [github.com/vectorforge22/NYPD-Shooting-Data-Analysis-Report](https://github.com/vectorforge22/NYPD-Shooting-Data-Analysis-Report). Corrections should identify the edition date, the affected claim or figure, and the evidence supporting the proposed change. A later source-data refresh should be issued as a new dated edition rather than silently changing the meaning of this snapshot.

## Accessibility

The Kindle edition uses real text, semantic headings, linked navigation, high-contrast figures, and textual interpretation adjacent to the charts. Colour is not intended to be the sole carrier of a conclusion. The fixed-layout PDF preserves the visual report, while the reflowable edition allows readers to adjust type size and reading settings. Source tables and reproducibility material remain available through the project repository.

## Edition history

- **Original coursework report, 25 January 2025:** historical source retained for provenance.
- **Revised publication edition, 18 September 2026:** corrected analytical units; refreshed official data through 30 June 2026; completed contextual analyses and forecast evaluation; added public-facing limitations, AI collaboration disclosure, credits, and Kindle publication structure.
